::: {.part}
Part four · being honest about it
:::

## What teaching people this actually does {#teaching .stop data-stop="teaching"}

::: {.year}
2026
:::

::: {.lead}
This whole page is an argument for explaining pain to people. So it is only fair to ask
what happens when somebody does that in a trial, and the answer is: less than the field
would like.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Khan and colleagues, 2026 [@khan26] — a systematic review and meta-analysis of **pain
neuroscience education**, which is the formal name for teaching people roughly what parts
one to three of this page teach. Twelve randomised trials, 1485 people.

The most honest number on this page. The effect on pain intensity is small, and its
confidence interval reaches exactly zero — the trials also disagreed with each other a
great deal. The sleep result is cleaner and the trials agreed on it. Read as a whole: this
does something, and it is not the large effect the enthusiasm around it suggests.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="pne"}
The bar is where the true effect probably sits. The pain bar reaches zero, which means "no
effect at all" has not been ruled out. The sleep bar does not reach it.
:::

The pain result is a standardised effect of **−0.27**, with a range from −0.50 to **0.00**.
In plain terms: on average people hurt somewhat less, the effect is small, and the evidence
is compatible with it doing nothing to pain at all. The trials also disagreed substantially
among themselves, which usually means the thing being tested was not the same thing in
every trial.

Total sleep time came out at **+0.42**, from 0.12 to 0.71, and there the trials agreed with
each other completely. It is the sturdier finding, and it is not the one anybody advertises.

We could have left this stop out. The page would have read better and been worse. If the
argument is *check what the evidence actually says*, that has to include checking it on the
thing the page is itself doing.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
Explaining pain well is worth doing, and it is not a treatment on its own. The trials that
did best combined it with movement and with the rest of care — which is roughly what you
were going to do anyway.
:::

## How much each of these can carry {#weights .stop data-stop="weights"}

::: {.year}
Now
:::

::: {.lead}
Every stop on this page rests on a source, and the sources are not equally good.
Flattening that would undo most of the point.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
All of it, weighed against each other. The placement below is **our judgement**, not a
measurement, and the caption says so — what it is for is the ordering.

The last entry deserves naming. A builder jumped onto a plank and a seven-inch nail went
through his boot. He was in agony and was sedated before the boot came off, at which point
the nail turned out to have passed cleanly between his toes without touching him
[@fisher95]. It is a wonderful story, and it is **one paragraph in a magazine column** —
no method, no follow-up, no imaging — retold in more lectures than most randomised trials.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="weights"}
A judgement, not a measurement. The value is the gradient: the best-supported things are
the least dramatic, and the most repeated story on the page sits at the bottom.
:::

Notice the shape of it. The claims near the top are boring — *findings that look like
damage are common in people with no pain*, *signals are turned up and down on the way in*.
The claims near the bottom are the ones that make a good lecture. That is not a coincidence
and it is not unique to this field, but it is worth being able to see.

The nail story is a good test of your own habits. It probably persuaded you when you first
heard it, and it should not have — not because it is false, but because a paragraph cannot
carry the weight of a general claim about how pain works. The scans in part two carry that
weight. The nail carries almost none of it, and gets repeated ten times as often.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
When you find yourself reaching for the most memorable example, check what it is made of.
The strongest thing you can say to a frightened client is not the dramatic anecdote — it is
the boring, replicated one about what ordinary backs look like.
:::
